title: Multi-Step Processes
summary: Coordinate workflows that must survive retries, partial failure, and time.
keyPoints: Some work spans many steps, services, and long waits, so one database transaction cannot cover it.
A saga records progress and uses compensating actions when a later step fails.
Orchestration centralizes control; choreography lets services react to events.
Durable execution engines checkpoint workflow state so a crash does not restart the whole process.
Every step needs an idempotency key, a timeout, and a bounded retry policy.
An append-only audit trail is part of the design, not an afterthought.

complexity.note: Best when one database covers every write.

commonMistakes: Holding a database transaction open while calling an external service.
Retrying a step without an idempotency key and creating a duplicate charge or shipment.
Treating a compensating action as a true rollback of an external effect.
Building a custom workflow engine before checking whether a single transaction or a queue would do.
interviewNotes: State which steps are local transactions and which call external systems.
Name the point of no return and the compensation for each reversible step.
Explain how a crash between an external call and the database write is detected and repaired.
Choose orchestration or choreography and give the reason.
Describe what happens to a workflow that exhausts its retries.

checkYourself.question: When is a single database transaction enough?
checkYourself.answer: When every write touches one database and the work finishes quickly, with no external call and no long wait. Locks and atomicity then cover the whole change.

checkYourself.question: Why is a compensation not a rollback?
checkYourself.answer: The original effect may be visible outside the database. A refund or a cancellation is a new action that offsets it; it cannot erase the first charge or an email that was sent.

checkYourself.question: What does a durable execution engine persist?
checkYourself.answer: Workflow state, step results, and timers. After a crash, a worker can resume from the last checkpoint instead of starting the workflow again.
